title: When a Fourier series converges
objectives: See that a Fourier series converges to the midpoint at a jump and overshoots beside it by a fixed share
Link smoothness to the decay of the coefficients and bound the error of a truncation

screens.prose: The square wave's partial sum uses odd terms up to $k = 2M - 1$. The view is zoomed in on the jump at $x = 0$. Set $M = 10$ and drag the dot to the top of the first peak beside the jump.
screens.question: How high is that peak? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: The curve overshoots the wave just to the right of the jump. Drag the dot there.
The peak is the highest point of the first bump.
For $M = 10$ it sits at $x = \pi/20 = 0.157$.

feedback.correct: At $M = 10$ the peak is 1.1798. At $M = 5$ it is 1.1823 and at $M = 50$ it is 1.1790.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag the dot to the top of the first bump and read its height.

byKey.wave: 1 is the height of the wave itself. The partial sum rises above it near the jump.
byKey.m5: 1.1823 is the peak for $M = 5$. Check that the control reads $M = 10$.

explain.text: With more terms the peak moves in towards the jump, from $\pi/10$ at $M = 5$ to $\pi/20$ at $M = 10$. Its height barely changes: 1.1823, 1.1798, 1.1790. It never falls below about 1.179.

screens.prose: The peak heights 1.1823, 1.1798 and 1.1790 tend to $\tfrac2\pi\mathrm{Si}(\pi) = 1.17898$. The wave jumps from $-1$ to $+1$, a jump of 2. The overshoot is the peak minus 1.
screens.question: What percentage of the jump of 2 is the overshoot? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: The overshoot is the extra height above 1: $1.17898 - 1$.
Compare it with the whole jump, from $-1$ to $+1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the overshoot $0.17898$ by the jump of 2.

byKey.of-height: 17.9% compares the overshoot with the wave's height 1. Gibbs's share is measured against the whole jump of 2.
byKey.peak: 117.9% is the peak as a share of the height. The overshoot is only the part above 1.

explain.text: The overshoot is $1.17898 - 1 = 0.17898$ and the jump is 2, so the share is 8.95%. This is Gibbs's phenomenon. The same share appears at every jump, whatever $M$.

screens.prose: How fast do coefficients fall? The plot has log axes, so a power law $k^{-s}$ is a straight line of slope $-s$. The upper line is the square wave's $|b_k| = \tfrac{4}{\pi k}$ for odd $k$. The lower line is the coefficient of $|x|$, which has a kink, not a jump.
screens.question: What is the slope of the lower line, for $|a_k| = \dfrac{4}{\pi k^2}$?

hints.text: On log axes, $\ln|a_k| = \ln\tfrac4\pi - 2\ln k$.
Compare how far each line falls between $k = 1$ and $k = 10$.
The lower line falls by a factor of 100 per factor of 10 in $k$.

feedback.correct: The slope is $-2$ for a kink and $-1$ for a jump.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\ln|a_k|$ as a straight line in $\ln k$ and read its slope.

byKey.minus-one: $-1$ is the slope of the upper line, the square wave. The kink gives $k^{-2}$.
byKey.plus-two: Coefficients fall as $k$ grows, so the slope is negative.

explain.text: $\ln|a_k| = \ln\tfrac{4}{\pi} - 2\ln k$ is a line of slope $-2$. A jump gives $-1$ and a kink gives $-2$. The smoother the function, the steeper the line.

screens.prose: Faster decay means faster convergence. The largest error of the $|x|$ series is at $x = 0$. There $|x| = 0$, so the error is just the partial sum. Slide $N$ and read the dot. Terms go up to $k = 2N - 1$.
screens.question: What is the error at $x = 0$ with $N = 5$, terms up to $k = 9$? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Set $N = 5$ and read the number beside the dot.
At $x = 0$ every cosine is 1, so the sum is $\pi/2 - \tfrac4\pi\sum 1/k^2$.
The odd terms to $k = 9$ sum to $1 + \tfrac19 + \tfrac1{25} + \tfrac1{49} + \tfrac1{81}$.

feedback.correct: With terms up to $k = 9$ the error is 0.0635.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $N = 5$ and read the dot at $x = 0$.

byKey.one-term: 0.2976 is the error with one term, $N = 1$. Check the slider.
byKey.n99: 0.0064 needs terms up to $k = 99$, which is $N = 50$.

explain.text: The errors at $x = 0$ are 0.2976 for one term, 0.0635 up to $k = 9$ and 0.0064 up to $k = 99$. Ten times the terms gives about ten times less error, because the tail adds up many coefficients. The square wave's error beside its jump does not shrink at all.

screens.prose: To say how many terms are enough we bound the tail. Each term $\tfrac1{k^2}$ with $k > N$ is less than the area under $\tfrac{1}{x^2}$ over the unit step that ends at $k$. So $\sum_{k > N}\tfrac{1}{k^2}$ is less than the area under $\tfrac{1}{x^2}$ from $N$ onwards.
screens.question: Write that area, from $N$ to infinity, in terms of $N$.

hints.text: An antiderivative of $x^{-2}$ is $-x^{-1}$.
The shaded area runs from $N$ to the right edge.
$\left[-\tfrac1x\right]_N^\infty = 0 + \tfrac1N$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $x^{-2}$ from $N$ to infinity.

byKey.squared: $1/N^2$ is the size of one term. The tail adds up many of them, and their sum is of order $1/N$.
byKey.half: $1/(2N^2)$ is the area under $1/x^3$. Here the integrand is $1/x^2$.
byKey.log: $\ln N$ is the area under $1/x$. For $1/x^2$ the integral converges.

explain.text: The integral gives $\tfrac1N$, so the tail is below $\tfrac1N$. For $N = 10$ the true tail is 0.095166, just under 0.1. So cutting the $|x|$ series after $k = K$ leaves an error below $\tfrac{4}{\pi K}$.

screens.prose: Energy is conserved by the series. For $f(x) = x$ the sines are orthogonal, so $\frac1\pi\int f^2\,dx = \sum b_k^2$. Use it to sum $\sum 1/k^2$. Leave out the two lines that do not belong.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: Square the series and integrate. Orthogonality kills every cross term $b_jb_k$ with $j \ne k$, and $\int\sin^2 kx = \pi$, so $\frac1\pi\int f^2 = \sum b_k^2$.
The cross terms $b_jb_k$ add a further positive amount, so $\sum b_k^2$ is less than the energy.
lines.why: Each cross term integrates to 0 by orthogonality. The squares alone account for all the energy.
$b_k = 2(-1)^{k+1}/k$, so $b_k^2 = 4/k^2$. The 2 is squared as well.

hints.text: Two routes to the same energy: the integral of $f^2$, and the sum of squared coefficients.
Compute both energies, then equate them.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line should follow from the line before it.

explain.text: The square of the series has only squared terms left, because the cross terms integrate to 0. Matching $2\pi^2/3$ against $4\sum 1/k^2$ gives Euler's sum $\pi^2/6 = 1.644934$. Convergence of the series in energy is exactly that identity.

screens.prose: A colleague says more terms must remove the overshoot, because the series converges at every point. Slide $M$ from 10 to 50 and watch the first peak. The valley between the wave and the peak narrows.
screens.question: What happens to the overshoot as $M$ grows?

options.text: It narrows towards the jump, but its height stays near 1.179
It shrinks towards the wave's height 1, since the series converges
options.why: The series does converge at every fixed $x$, but the peak slides towards the jump at the same pace. Its height stays.

options.text: It grows without limit as the terms pile up near the jump
options.why: It does not grow either. Its height settles at 1.17898, about 8.95% of the jump above the wave.

hints.text: Compare the first peak at $M = 10$ and at $M = 50$.
The heights are 1.1798 and 1.1790.
The peak sits near $x = \pi/(2M)$ and its height tends to 1.17898.

feedback.correct: The peak moves in, near $x = \pi/(2M)$, but its height stays near 1.179.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the height of the first peak at two values of $M$.

byKey.shrinks: You expected the peak to settle onto the wave. At each fixed $x$ it does, but a peak that always stays beside the jump keeps its height.
byKey.grows: The peak neither shrinks nor grows. It tends to 1.17898 as $M$ rises.

explain.text: For any fixed $x > 0$ the sum tends to 1, since the peak passes it by. But the peak itself sits near $x = \pi/(2M)$ and keeps its height of about 1.179. The convergence is pointwise, not uniform near the jump.

screens.prose: Edge case. The function $f(x) = x$ is smooth on $(-\pi, \pi)$. The series treats it as a wave that repeats every $2\pi$. At $x = \pi$ it jumps from $\pi$ back to $-\pi$. Its series is $\sum\tfrac{2(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\sin kx$.
screens.question: What does the series give at $x = \pi$?

widget.accept: 0: every $\sin k\pi$ is 0, the midpoint of $\pi$ and $-\pi$.
widget.label: Series value

hints.text: Put $x = \pi$ into each term of the series.
The dot sits at $x = \pi$.
$\sin k\pi = 0$ for every whole $k$.

feedback.correct: Every term has $\sin k\pi = 0$, so the series gives 0, the midpoint of the jump.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute $x = \pi$ into $\sin kx$.

byKey.f: 3.1416 is $f(\pi)$. The series does not see $f$ alone: it sees the repeating wave, which jumps there.
byKey.minus: $-\pi$ is the value just beyond the jump. At the jump itself the series takes the midpoint.

explain.text: The repeating extension jumps by $2\pi$ at $x = \pi$, so the series takes the midpoint 0. It rings beside the jump, though $f$ is smooth. Any $f$ that differs at its two ends makes such a jump.

screens.prose: Measure both effects. `gibbs_peak(M)` returns the largest partial sum of the square wave on $(0, \pi/2]$, from a grid of $n$ points. It keeps odd terms up to $k = 2M - 1$. `decay_slope(b, ks)` fits $\ln|b_k|$ against $\ln k$.

hints.text: Add the terms one at a time into an array the same size as `x`.
Term $j$ has $k = 2j - 1$ and size $4/(\pi k)$.
`np.polyfit(np.log(ks), np.log(abs(b)), 1)` returns the slope first.

feedback.correct: The peaks match 1.182328, 1.179814 and 1.179013, and the slopes are exactly $-1$ and $-2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the odd $k$, the sign handling in `abs`, and the order `polyfit` returns.

explain.text: The peak tends to 1.17898 as $M$ grows, though the location moves in. The slope of $\ln|b_k|$ is the power in $|b_k| \propto k^{-s}$: $-1$ for the square wave and $-2$ for $|x|$.

screens.prose: You have seen **convergence of a Fourier series**. At a point where $f$ is continuous the series converges to $f$. At a jump it converges to the midpoint of the two sides. Near a jump the partial sums overshoot by about 8.95% of the jump, however many terms. A smoother $f$ has faster-decaying coefficients.
screens.question: The square wave jumps from $-1$ to $+1$ at $x = 0$. What does its series converge to at $x = 0$?

options.why: The series is the same from either side, so it cannot pick the right-hand value. Every term $\sin k\cdot 0$ is 0.
It converges, to the midpoint. Only the overshoot nearby fails to settle.

feedback.correct: Every term has $\sin 0 = 0$, and the midpoint of $-1$ and $1$ is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $x = 0$ into the series, and compare with the midpoint.

explain.text: At $x = 0$ each term $\tfrac{4}{k\pi}\sin(k\cdot 0)$ is 0, so the series gives 0, the midpoint of $-1$ and $1$. This is the rule for every jump.

screens.prose: A Fourier pricer keeps $N$ terms of the payoff's series. A digital payoff jumps, so its coefficients fall like $1/k$. A call has a kink, so its coefficients fall like $1/k^2$. At $N = 20$ the first dropped coefficient is 0.01 for both. The picture has log axes.
screens.question: At what $N$ is the call's first dropped coefficient 0.0001?

widget.accept: 200: the coefficient falls 100 times, and $1/k^2$ needs $k$ ten times larger.
widget.label: Terms $N$

hints.text: The call's coefficients fall like $1/k^2$. Find the factor they must fall.
The steeper line on the plot is the call.
A factor of 100 in size is a factor of $\sqrt{100} = 10$ in $N$.

feedback.correct: $N = 20 \times 10 = 200$ for the call. The digital would need 2,000.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Coefficients fall like $1/k^2$, so a hundredfold drop needs $k$ to grow by $\sqrt{100}$.

byKey.digital-rule: 2,000 is the answer for the digital, whose coefficients fall like $1/k$. The call falls faster, like $1/k^2$.
byKey.hundred: 100 would give a coefficient of $0.01\times(20/100)^2 = 0.0004$. Not yet small enough.

explain.text: For the call, size $= 0.01\,(20/N)^2$, and 0.0001 gives $N = 200$. For the digital, size $= 0.01\,(20/N)$ and $N = 2{,}000$. The heat factor $e^{-k^2t}$ removes the difference for any $t > 0$, as the next lesson shows.

ideas: At a point where $f$ is continuous the series converges to $f$. At a jump it converges to the midpoint of the two sides.
Beside a jump the partial sums overshoot by about 8.95% of the jump however many terms. The overshoot narrows towards the jump but keeps its height.
A jump gives coefficients of size $1/k$, a kink gives $1/k^2$. Smoother functions converge faster, and Parseval gives $\sum 1/k^2 = \pi^2/6$.

formula.name: Gibbs overshoot
formula.note: For the square wave of height 1: the peak sits near $x = \pi/(2M)$.

summary.trap: More terms narrow the overshoot but do not lower it: the peak stays near 1.179.

quiz.prose: The sum of all $1/k^2$ is $\pi^2/6$. The even terms $1/(2j)^2$ are a quarter of the full sum.
quiz.question: What is the sum of $1/k^2$ over odd $k$ only? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the even terms away from the full sum.

byKey.even: 0.4112 is the sum over even $k$. The odd terms are what remains.
byKey.all: 1.6449 is the sum over every $k$. Remove the even terms.

explain.text: The even terms sum to $\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac{\pi^2}{6} = 0.4112$. The odd terms are the rest: $1.6449 - 0.4112 = 1.2337$. That is $\pi^2/8$.

quiz.prose: A payoff $f$ equals 2 just left of $x = a$ and 8 just right of it. Its Fourier series converges there.
quiz.question: What value does the series take at $x = a$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At a jump the series takes the midpoint.

byKey.left: 2 is the left-hand limit. The series favours neither side and takes the midpoint.
byKey.right: 8 is the right-hand limit. The series favours neither side.

explain.text: The series is built from smooth waves, which see both sides equally. At the jump it settles at the midpoint, 5. Near the jump it overshoots by 8.95% of the jump of 6.

quiz.prose: Three periodic functions are expanded in Fourier series.
quiz.question: Which has the fastest-decaying coefficients?

options.why: A jump gives $1/k$, the slowest decay of the three.
A kink gives $1/k^2$. A smooth function does better, faster than any power of $k$.

feedback.correct: The smoother the function, the faster the coefficients decay.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rank the functions by smoothness.

explain.text: A jump gives $1/k$ and a kink gives $1/k^2$. A smooth periodic function gives faster than any power. That is why smooth payoffs are cheap to price by Fourier methods.

quiz.prose: The first peak of the square wave's partial sum sits near $x = \pi/(2M)$, as the hook showed for $M = 5$ and $M = 10$.
quiz.question: Where does it sit for $M = 100$? Give 4 decimal places.

byKey.m50: 0.0314 is $\pi/100$, which drops the 2 in $2M$. It is also the place for $M = 50$.
byKey.height: 1.179 is the peak's height, not where it sits.

explain.text: $\pi/(2M)$ is $0.157$ for $M = 10$ and 0.0157 for $M = 100$. The peak hugs the jump ever more closely but keeps its height.
